newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Caribbean islands brace for American strike.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean islands brace for American strike.

text.p: A sense of urgency replaced the laid-back calm of the Caribbean winter Tuesday, as travellers, governments and businesses braced themselves for a looming strike at American Airlines.

Officials said a walkout Friday night at the AMR Corp. airline, by far the most important carrier in the region, would be difficult at any time, but devastating at the height of the winter tourist season.

"Our members are terrified with a strike occurring because American Airlines and American Eagle together have 70 percent of the airlift into the region. If there's a strike, you are talking about big layoffs, closures and massive losses of revenue," said John Bell, executive vice president of the Caribbean Hotel Association.
He estimated that an American strike would cost the Caribbean tourism industry a minimum of $15 million a day.

At San Juan's Luis Munoz Marin International Airport, American's Caribbean hub, security and maintenance crews were doubled. And the government convened a task force and set up a special centre with 18 telephone lines to assist anyone left stranded by the loss of American's 52 flights a day and try to arrange flights on carriers including USAir, Continental Airlines, Pan American and TWA.

"The majority of tourists who stay in our hotels come to the island as passengers on American Airlines," said Erin Benitez, executive director of the Puerto Rico Hotel & Tourism Association, who noted that 1996-1997 has been one of the best winter tourism seasons in years.
"The effects of such a strike on our tourism season would be devastating," she said. Tourism accounts for about 8 percent of Puerto Rico's gross national product.

The carrier is also a major force in Puerto Rico's air cargo, complementing the island's giant sea port by carrying everything from mail to some of the pharmaceuticals and other products used at the island's many manufacturing plants.

"It's going to reduce the space available for cargo, so yes we are very concerned," said Hector Jimenez, the executive vice president of the Puerto Rico Manufacturers Association. "The only thing we can do now is bring as much raw material and other products to the island as possible and wait."

Last minute preparations also were under way in the nearby U.S. Virgin Islands, which also relies on American to ferry in tourists, and were still reeling from the effects of Hurricane Marilyn in September 1995 and the loss of Prestige Airline service as of Jan. 15, 1997.
"The loss of Americans' service would wreak havoc on the tourism season," said Beverly Nicholson, executive director of the St. Thomas-St. John Hotel Association. "We are extremely concerned."
The Virgin Island's earnings from tourism come to about $800 million a year, or about 70 percent of its non-oil revenues.

In the Cayman Islands, the upscale tourist destination south of Cuba, officials estimated the American strike could cost the islands almost $5 million each day the a strike lasted. With 21 flights and 3,426 passenger seats each week from Miami, American had been flying to the Caymans with 90 percent occupancy.

To help fill the void, Cayman Airways, the national flag carrier, anounced it would add three Miami-Cayman daily flights, to complement its current three flights. "Luckily, we probably won't be as bad off as some Caribbean destinations who don't have a national airline to step in and take up the slack," Doug Sears, vice president of the Cayman Islands Hotel & Condominium Association, said.
But he noted that tourists will have to get to Miami -- where American has 200 flights per day -- to connect to the Cayman carrier.

On Tuesday, AMR and its 10,000 pilots were in talks to try to avert the strike set for midnight on Friday, which would shut down the second-largest U.S. carrier and strand hundreds of thousands of passengers worldwide.
